name: Elias of Nisibis
knownFor: The metropolitan of Nisibis in the Church of the East who wrote the Chronography, a year-by-year record that E. W. Brooks dates to 1019. For most years it names its sources, and most of those are lost.
dates: Born 975, by a note later hands added to his Chronography. E. W. Brooks dates the Chronography to 1019, and M.-A. Kugener to 1008. Joseph Assemani puts his death after 1049, J.-B. Chabot soon after it; Frédéric Macler gives about 1056. The note's years are reckoned from its Greek and Arab years
place: Nisibis; earlier Beth Nuhadra. He was ordained priest at the monastery of Father Simeon, facing Senn in Brooks's Latin
tradition: The Church of the East under the Abbasids
role: Metropolitan of Nisibis; chronicler and writer

keyWorks.title: Chronography
keyWorks.about: in two parts. The first holds lists of patriarchs and kings, a short history of the catholicoi, and year-by-year tables, most years naming their sources. The second sets out how peoples reckon their years and feasts

keyWorks.title: Grammar
keyWorks.about: a Syriac grammar in ten headings, on letters, points and sounds. Assemani says a Syriac-Arabic word list by Elias follows it

keyWorks.title: Four books on judging church cases
keyWorks.about: named in the catalogue of Ebedjesu of Soba, as Assemani prints it, and by J.-B. Chabot. Ebedjesu copied Elias's preface, and the rules on inheritance he gathered from the catholicos Elias I, into his collection of canons, held in Angelo Mai's Latin

traces: E. W. Brooks lists the works the Chronography cites, Greek, Syriac and Arabic, and says most of them are lost.
Passages of Jacob of Edessa's chronicle, which E. W. Brooks calls partly lost, survive in his quotations. The Chronica Minora prints them as Jacob's testimonies quoted by Elias.
J. Parisot notes that a British Museum manuscript gives the Chronography in Syriac and Arabic.
remembered: Joseph Assemani writes that he died having won great fame for learning among his people.
Ebedjesu of Soba calls him a most exact and sharp-minded man, who told all lovers of truth to follow the catholicos Elias I's treatise on inheritance alone.
George David Malech lists him, as Elias Bar Shinaji, among the Syrian forebears whose writings trace their nation from Shem.
J. B. Abbeloos and T. J. Lamy, editing Bar Hebraeus's church history, often cite him on dates.

uncertain: His life is told in a note that later hands added to his Chronography, and in Assemani, who draws one detail from Elias's own words.
When he wrote the Chronography. E. W. Brooks dates it to 1019. M.-A. Kugener dates it to 1008, and says the British Museum copy was made in Elias's own time.
When he died. In a preface on inheritance, Elias prays for the soul of the catholicos Elias I, who died in 1049. Assemani puts his death after that, and Chabot soon after. Macler gives about 1056.

The Isho'yahb affair. Assemani says Elias opposed Isho'yahb son of Ezekiel and called him a simoniac. The letter itself is not among the sources used here. Angelo Mai describes a Vatican manuscript that holds it.
Peace with Elias I. Mari ibn Sulayman says Elias I kept writing to the metropolitan of Nisibis until they met at Hazza and made peace. Mari does not name the metropolitan.
Why he wrote the second part. J.-B. Chabot thinks it not unlikely that al-Biruni's book on reckoning moved him to write. Chabot adds that Elias seems to have taken nothing from it.
Where he was a monk. Assemani, citing Elias's own words, says he was a monk at Saint Michael's near Mosul. The note says only that he was ordained priest at the monastery of Father Simeon.
